opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because I think people forget how compute-constrained that era actually felt. When the original AlphaGo was being built, around 2015 and 2016, the team wasn't operating with the mindset of "just scale it up and it'll work." Compute was precious. The system they built was quite intricate: supervised learning on human expert games to bootstrap a policy network, then reinforcement learning through self-play to improve it, then a value network, and all of it stitched together with Monte Carlo tree search. A lot of that machinery was there because you couldn't afford to brute-force your way to superhuman play from scratch.

So compute efficiency wasn't an afterthought. It was baked into the design. Starting from human data was a way of saving compute. You give the network a reasonable prior so the search doesn't waste cycles exploring obviously terrible moves. The value network was another efficiency trick: instead of rolling out every game to the end, you learn to estimate who's winning and prune the tree much earlier.

What's interesting, looking back, is that the lineage after that, AlphaGo Zero and then AlphaZero, went in the direction of stripping out the human scaffolding and leaning more on general learning plus search. In some sense that was more compute-hungry up front, but it was also more elegant and ended up being more efficient in the sense that matters. The algorithm was simpler, so each unit of compute bought you more real improvement.

I think that's the lesson I keep coming back to. There are two kinds of efficiency. There's the clever, hand-engineered kind, where you inject a lot of domain knowledge to save cycles. Then there's the kind where you find a simpler, more general recipe that scales gracefully when you throw more compute at it. Early on you almost always need the first kind just to get something working at all. But over time the second kind tends to win, and that's basically the bitter lesson playing out in miniature. AlphaGo was a beautiful example of both phases happening within just a couple of years.

r001.rationale: The response says compute efficiency was central to AlphaGo’s design and describes techniques chosen to save compute. Its remark about getting something working does not establish that this took priority over compute optimality during development.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I wasn't on the AlphaGo team, so I'm speaking as someone who watched it from the outside, but I think the compute efficiency story there is a little different from how people usually tell it.

At the time, the headline was that AlphaGo used something like 1,200 CPUs and a couple hundred GPUs to play Lee Sedol, and people pointed at that as this enormous, almost brute-force expenditure. And in one sense it was. But the deeper lesson was that the compute was being spent in the right place. Monte Carlo tree search had existed for years, and people had been throwing CPU time at Go for a long time without getting anywhere close to professional strength. What changed was that the neural networks gave you a much better prior over moves and a much better value estimate, so every unit of search compute became dramatically more valuable. In that sense it was a story about compute efficiency, not just compute scale: the policy network collapsed the branching factor, and the value network let you stop rolling out to the end of the game.

The other thing that I think gets lost is that the inefficiency was deliberate. When you're trying to prove that something is possible for the first time, you don't optimize. You spend whatever it takes to get the result, because the existence proof is the whole point. And then AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero came along afterward and showed you could get a stronger player on a single machine with a handful of TPUs, no human data, simpler algorithm. That's the usual pattern in this field. The first version is wildly wasteful, and then the efficiency gains come very fast once people know what they're aiming for.

So I'd say compute efficiency mattered a lot, but it mattered as a second step. If the AlphaGo team had been obsessing over efficiency from day one, I don't think they'd have gotten there in 2016. The trick is knowing which phase you're in.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that proving the first result was possible was the priority, so the team spent what it took rather than optimizing efficiency.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between making something work for the first time and making it efficient enough to deploy broadly. With the first AlphaGo, the central question was whether you could get a system to beat the best human players at all. If that took a lot of compute, that was a reasonable price to pay to establish that the approach worked.

Efficiency still mattered, because it determined how quickly you could run experiments and how much search you could do during a game. But you wouldn’t want to constrain the project to the compute budget of a consumer product before you’d demonstrated the capability. First you find a recipe that works; then you can figure out which parts are essential and make it cheaper.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the first priority was establishing that AlphaGo could beat top human players at all, and that using substantial compute was reasonable before optimizing cost.

sol-6.1.text:
I think compute efficiency matters a lot, but you have to be careful about what you’re optimizing for. When the first AlphaGo was being developed, the big question was whether you could make the system work at all. It was reasonable to spend a lot of compute to answer that question, even if the first version wasn’t particularly economical.

And algorithmic progress can completely change the economics afterward. A better policy or value network means you don’t have to search as much to make a good decision. So I wouldn’t frame it as efficiency versus scale. You use the compute you have to find something that works, and then the insights from that system help you build something much more efficient.

r001.rationale: It says the key question was whether AlphaGo could work at all and that spending substantial compute was reasonable, even if the first version was uneconomical.
